sections.h2: Which offices deal with a Jefferson County tax bill?
sections.html:
Three offices share the work in Jefferson County: the property appraiser values parcels, the tax collector bills and collects, and the clerk keeps the deed records and runs tax deed auctions. The county's own property and taxes page sends residents to jeffersonpa.net to search parcels and file for exemptions.

The county page also explains the August cycle. The appraiser mails a TRIM notice showing the property's value and the proposed rates from the county, the school board, the water management districts and other taxing bodies, and the public hearings listed on it come before rates are adopted in September. The city of Monticello levies its own rate, which appears as a separate line in the tax collector's millage list, so a bill inside city limits has more lines than one outside them.

  • Property Appraiser: values land and buildings, takes exemption filings, mails the notice of proposed taxes.
  • Tax Collector: mails statements on or before November 1, takes payment, advertises delinquent accounts, sells certificates.
  • Clerk and Comptroller: official records, and the public auction if a tax deed application is filed.

sections.h2: What is the Jefferson County billing calendar?
sections.html:
Statements go out on or before November 1, and paying in November earns a 4 percent discount that steps down to 1 percent in February. The tax collector's page states that taxes become delinquent on April 1 of each year.

Jefferson County tax collector calendar for real estate tax
WhenWhat the collector's page says
On or before November 1Tax statements mailed
November4 percent discount
December3 percent discount
January2 percent discount
February1 percent discount
April 1Delinquent, 3 percent penalty on unpaid real estate tax
Early MayUnpaid accounts advertised in the local paper
On or before June 1Online tax certificate sale

The collector's glossary adds that the lien for a year's tax attaches each January 1 and that taxes are payable before April 1 of the following year. Tangible personal property, such as business equipment and mobile home attachments, carries a heavier penalty of 1.5 percent per month once delinquent.

sections.h2: What is the Jefferson County millage rate for 2026?
sections.html:
The collector's millage page lists six lines for 2026, and a house inside Monticello would see all of them. The numbers print as decimals, so the county line reads .00736730, which is 7.3673 mills.

  • Jefferson County: .00736730
  • School, required local effort: .00316000
  • School, discretionary: .00224800
  • City of Monticello: .00685010
  • Northwest Florida Water Management District: .00002010
  • Suwannee River Water Management District: .00026950

The collector's page explains who sets each piece: the county commission sets the county rate, the school board sets the school rates, the city council sets the city rate, and special districts set their own. Those figures are the collector's published list, not a quote for your parcel. Ask the tax collector which lines apply to your address, since a rural parcel outside the city would not carry the Monticello line, and non-ad valorem charges for services appear separately on the bill.

sections.h2: What homestead and other exemptions can a Jefferson County owner claim?
sections.html:
The county's property page says the appraiser administers exemptions, homestead included. The state revenue department puts the homestead exemption at up to $50,000, filed on Form DR-501 by March 1, for an owner who made the home a permanent residence by January 1.

The first $25,000 applies to every tax, school tax included. The additional exemption of up to $25,000 reaches only value above $50,000 and only non-school taxes. Renting the home or ceasing to live there ends homestead. For an older owner, a county or city ordinance may add an extra exemption of up to $50,000 within an income limit, and the state lists benefits for disabled veterans and for deployed servicemembers on its exemption pages.

Ask the Jefferson County Property Appraiser which of those local options the county has adopted, because the state pages only describe what a local government may choose. Save Our Homes caps the yearly rise in a homestead's assessed value at the lower of 3 percent or the CPI change, and a sale resets the property to just value the next January 1.

sections.h2: How does the tax bill affect a Jefferson County sale?
sections.html:
The seller owes tax through the closing date, and any delinquent balance has to be paid off before the buyer can take clean title. Title companies normally request a payoff from the collector and settle the account out of the proceeds.

Jefferson County's collector warns that the tax roll is a working roll and figures can change during the year, so a quoted amount is a snapshot. That matters if you sell in the fall, when new statements are about to be mailed. Ask for a written payoff dated close to closing. Escrow accounts complicate this further: if a lender pays the bill, ask the servicer for the refund timeline on any unused escrow balance, since that money comes back to the seller after the loan is paid off and not at the table.

  • Search the parcel on the collector's site and note every year with a balance.
  • Ask whether a certificate was sold on any year, since a certificate needs to be redeemed with certified funds.
  • Confirm exemptions with the appraiser so the title company prorates correctly.
  • Record the deed with the clerk, who collects documentary stamp tax when it is recorded.

On deeds, state law sets doc stamps at 70 cents per $100 of consideration, and no party can escape liability by pointing at the contract.

sections.h2: What happens to unpaid Jefferson County property tax?
sections.html:
The county sells a tax certificate on the debt, and the owner then has a limited window before the parcel can go to a tax deed sale. The collector says a certificate is a lien created by paying the delinquent tax, not a purchase of the property.

The Jefferson County page describes the sale as a reverse auction on interest, starting at 18 percent and awarded to the lowest bidder. Certificates last seven years, and the face amount includes the 3 percent penalty, the 5 percent collector's commission and advertising costs. A homestead parcel whose face value is under $250 is issued to the county at 18 percent a year instead of being sold. Redemption requires certified funds, and the page warns that failing to redeem within the 22-month period can lead to loss of the property at a tax deed sale.

A holder may apply for a tax deed two years after April 1 of the year of issue. The clerk then runs the auction, and under state law the opening bid on homestead land includes half of the latest assessed value. An owner at risk should contact the collector's office right away and ask about the deferral program, which has a March 31 application date.

faqs.q: When do Jefferson County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: They become delinquent on April 1 each year, and the tax collector's page says a 3 percent penalty is added to unpaid real estate tax at that point.

faqs.q: What is the Jefferson County discount for paying early?
faqs.a: It is 4 percent in November, 3 percent in December, 2 percent in January and 1 percent in February, according to the tax collector. Statements are mailed on or before November 1.

faqs.q: Where do I file for homestead in Jefferson County?
faqs.a: File with the Jefferson County Property Appraiser by March 1. The county's property page directs residents to jeffersonpa.net, and the state form is DR-501.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Jefferson County house that has a tax certificate on it?
faqs.a: Yes, but the certificate has to be redeemed from the proceeds, and the collector requires certified funds. Get a payoff figure from the collector first.

faqs.q: Does the Jefferson County millage include the city of Monticello?
faqs.a: Only for parcels inside the city. The collector's 2026 list shows a separate Monticello line of .00685010 beside the county, school and water district lines.
